item.title: Judges say no requirement to help Gazans travel to NL
item.description:
Judges say no requirement to help Gazans travel to NL

November 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Netherlands is not required to provide consular services to Gazans who are unable to travel abroad to obtain Dutch entry visas, a judge ruled on Friday.

The case revolves around 111 people currently living in Gaza who have been granted entry visas to the Netherlands.

Documents must be picked up in person and the Dutch have no consular presence in the enclave, so people have to travel abroad to obtain their visas.

The lawsuit argued that it is nearly impossible for Gazans to travel to Jordan to get their visas and the Dutch have an obligation to assist them in travelling to the embassy.

A judge at the District Court of The Hague disagreed, ruling that “there is no entitlement to consular assistance.”

The decision noted that the outcome would hit the plaintiffs hard, but “the decision to help the plaintiffs in Gaza is reserved for the political sphere and not for the court.”

item.title: VVD ministers rally round Yesilgöz ahead of party congress
item.description:
VVD ministers rally round Yesilgöz ahead of party congress

November 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Members of the right-wing liberal VVD party have flocked to defend their leader Dilan Yesilgöz after mounting criticism of her leadership and her dual status as party leader and defence minister, as well as the recent cabinet crisis, led to speculation she could be ousted, ahead of the party’s congress on Saturday.

Prime minister Rob Jetten, whose minority cabinet was on the brink of collapse earlier this month after Yesilgöz described the government as a “failed experiment”, also spoke in favour of her on Friday, saying “I have every confidence that her fighting spirit will serve her well at the congress”, according to Het Parool.

The VVD’s former chair Christianne van der Wal spoke on TV talk show Pauw & De Wit earlier this week saying that there was “enormous discontent” within the party rank and file, but that loyalty kept criticism largely under wraps. She said that Yesilgöz’s dual role was a particular point of contention.

But Jetten said this is perfectly normal in Dutch politics and that her roles are well compatible.

The criticism levelled by Van der Wal led to doubts over Yesilgöz’s continued leadership in the build-up to Saturday’s VVD congress, where party issues will be discussed after a turbulent few weeks.

The Volkskrant also reported that VVD members are concerned about the provincial elections next March.

Despite the media pressure building around Yesilgöz, Friday’s cabinet meeting saw VVD members come out in support of her.

“I know no one who works harder than she does,” infrastructure minister Vincent Karremans said.

“I work closely with Dilan and I think she combines her various roles well,” health minister Sophie Hermans told the Volkskrant.

Yesilgöz avoided the press and gave no comment after Friday’s meeting, NOS said.

item.title: Dutch destinations: an autumn getaway in Middelburg, Zeeland
item.description:
Dutch destinations: an autumn getaway in Middelburg, Zeeland

November 27, 2026 Robin Pascoe

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch flock to Zeeland in the summer to take advantage of the wide beaches, the seafood and hopefully the sunshine. But it is also a great location for an autumn or winter break, with the provincial capital Middelburg making the perfect base.

Middelburg, on the former island of Walcheren, can trace its history back to 880 and was awarded city rights in 1217, making it nearly 100 years older than Amsterdam.

In 1585 Middelburg opened its gates to refugees after the fall of Antwerp in the Eighty Years’ War with Spain, and the Flemish influence is still palpable in some of the architecture. In 1705 the first chocolate mill was set up on the outskirts of the city and its railway station opened in 1872.

Today its medieval centre is elegant, compact and well worth a wander around. Check out the names of the houses along the Rotterdamsekaai and the area around the magnificent Oostkerk, which now hosts concerts, and you will see plenty of testimonials to its past. We spotted an Edinburg and an Edenberg, a Groot Brittangie, a Spaerpot (piggy bank) and a strangely named “de twee harde Bollen” among the signage.

Five things to do

Stroll through the Abdij
Middelburg’s centre is dominated by its abbey, an impressive complex of buildings, with a garden, various towers and a wide, tree-filled square which is used to host cultural events. The abbey dates back to 1100 when the first parts were built by the Norbertine monks. Today it is home to the provincial council offices and the Zeeuws Museum. Note, the Lange Jan tower is closed to the public for the winter season.

Visit a museum
The Zeeuws Museum is one of our favourite provincial museums because it does not overwhelm you with information and is happily lacking in infotainment. The first two floors are devoted to temporary exhibitions and the third floor focuses on the history of the province. Carefully selected objects – children’s cloth caps, pottery, portraits of notables – nod to important stages in the city’s past.

The top floor has three “cabinets of curiosities” compiled from the museum’s collection such as the skeleton of a cat coupled with pottery moggies from 1850. It’s easy to cover the entire museum in a couple of hours.

Catch up on Christmas shopping
Middelburg has a main drag full of the brands you would expect, interspersed with local stores and a number of specialty outlets such as a store selling kites and juggler’s equipment. There are several chocolate specialists to choose from and wine shops selling local Zeeland wine.

For souvenirs, pick up some Zeeuwse bolus – a sticky spiral pastry with cinnamon and dark brown sugar or a packet of Boterbabbelaar, a buttery sort of toffee.

Walk in the woods
De Manteling is a coastal nature reserve near the seaside resort of Domburg, some 15 minutes’ drive from Middelburg. It is based around several former country estates, the main one of which is now a youth hostel. There are several routes to follow winding through the oak forest, and the blue one, which is four kilometres long, will take you out to the beach.

Visit Veere
Only 10 minutes from Middelburg by car, the village of Veere used to be open to the sea, and its wealth stems from its position as a major port in the wool trade with Scotland back in the 15th century. The splendid Schotse Huizen museum on the waterfront is well worth a visit and goes into this history in more detail. Veere gets very busy with coach parties in the summer.

Where to eat
Middelburg has masses of places to eat, and you would be advised to book if you plan to have dinner in one of the more highly-rated places. Lots of cafés and restaurants are based around the main market square, where you can get a burger, ribs or local fish. The Herberg is a favourite with the locals and offers more adventurous fare. You’ll find more choice on the Dam next to the abbey.

We had lunch at Brasserie 1600 which was pretty standard for a Dutch café lunch – croquettes on bread, warm goat’s cheese broodjes – but cheaper than the big cities and with friendlier staff.

In the evening we ate at the Packhuys on the Kinderdijk which offers an interesting seafood-based tasting menu of four to seven courses in a converted warehouse. Restaurant Scherp is in a city centre townhouse and also has two rooms where guests can stay. Basalt also comes highly recommended.

Where to stay
There are lots of options in Middelburg but you would do well to book up in plenty of time for your trip if you are coming at the weekend. It’s a popular place.

We stayed in a “city loft” in Hotel St Joris, which originally dates from 1582 and is close to the abbey walls, and paid €156 for the night including breakfast by booking directly. Ask for a room on the first two floors if you are not good with stairs. The nearby Poorthuys B&B comes highly recommended, as does the Zilver Reiger.

How to get there
It takes about two hours to reach Middelburg by car from Amsterdam, depending on the traffic, and there is plenty of parking on the edge of town. Inner city parking is pricey and nothing is far away on foot. There are regular trains from Amsterdam and The Hague, and you can pick up an OV-fiets (bike) at the station if you want to explore the countryside.

Anything else
When we were in Middelburg, in late November, the Stadhuis, or town hall, was wrapped in scaffolding as part of a major renovation project. The main market square had also been filled with an artificial ice rink and the café terraces had been turned into ski chalets for the winter season.

item.title: Prosecutors open investigation into neo-Nazi cage fights
item.description:
Prosecutors open investigation into neo-Nazi cage fights

November 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The prosecution service has begun an investigation into the neo-Nazi events that were exposed by a Zembla documentary last week, in which politicians, teachers and a health care professionals were seen attending cage fighting tournaments organised by extreme-right groups.

Since the documentary was released, which was based on an undercover investigation, six members of the far-right FVD have been expelled from the party.

A Rotterdam lecturer who acted as a medic, a high school teacher and a psychiatrist were also identified. The psychiatrist has also worked as an expert witness in judicial cases and previously had a firearms licence.

The footage shows members repeatedly throwing up Nazi salutes and shouting Sieg Heil, and members of one group holding an annual commemoration for Adolf Hitler in Luxembourg.

The former chief of the Dutch national intelligence agency AIVD, Rob Bertholee, told news programme Nieuwsuur that the groups and neo-Nazi symbols should be banned. The issue is that they were held as private events. Public displays of Nazi symbology can be punished in some cases.

Bertholee also said investigating connections between political parties and neo-Nazi organisations is complicated. Individuals can be held to account but investigating inherent links with entire political organisations, as some have called for with the FVD, would be sensitive.

A total ban would be easier said than done because of freedom of speech, he said, but he also voiced concerns that the far-right ideology is spreading throughout society. “We used to associate the far right with skinheads. We know now: people who adhere to this ideology look like anyone and can practice any profession.”

item.title: Abattoirs face closure for threatening and abusing inspectors
item.description:
Abattoirs face closure for threatening and abusing inspectors

November 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Junior agriculture minister Silvio Erkens wants start shutting down slaughterhouses if inspectors are threatened there. This follows revelations recently that food safety authority workers are afraid to inspect some abattoirs because of the violence and intimidation they face.

Erkens told MPs during Wednesday’s debate on the agriculture budget that one option was a three-strikes principle, under which a slaughterhouse could be closed after, for example, three violations, broadcaster NOS reported.

“There should be no place in the Netherlands for slaughterhouses like this,” he said, though he did not name any particular culprits.

In the debate, Erkens said inspectors had reported intimidating phone calls, threats and being followed, sometimes by someone with a guard dog, and in some cases even into the toilet. Staff had also faced discrimination, physical aggression, and sexual intimidation, and some had been targeted in their private lives along with their families.

“It happens too often and too widely,” Erkens said, adding that these were not isolated incidents. He declined to name the slaughterhouses involved.

The NVWA can already halt slaughter at a plant until a problem is resolved. Erkens said that made sense for a single incident, but that a pattern called for a permanent solution.

MPs from left-wing PRO, the anti-immigration PVV, the Party for the Animals (PvdD), and centrist D66 had urged him the day before to take tougher action rather than rely on talks with the meat industry. Erkens said appealing to the sector had not worked.

He said he would set out early next year whether the legislation will go ahead and how it would work.

item.title: Ghanaian artist kąrî’kạchä seid’ou wins Prince Claus award
item.description:
Ghanaian artist kąrî’kạchä seid’ou wins Prince Claus award

November 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

“A rebel with a strong cause.” That’s how prince Constantijn described Ghanaian artist and poet kąrî’kạchä seid’ou when presenting the Prince Claus Fund 2026 Impact Award on Thursday.

Set up in 1996 as a 70th birthday gift for the late husband of princess Beatrix, the fund awards international artists and creators in places “where cultural expression is under pressure”.

“Known for his radical and democratic approaches to artistic practice and teaching, seid’ou has been a key catalyst for artistic innovation in Ghana and across West Africa since the early 1990s,” the fund said.

According to NOS, seid’ou, who was born in 1968, does not believe that art needs to meet any conditions, and is less concerned with exhibitions or sales than with how artists are trained.

seid’ou travelled outside the African continent for the first time to accept his 50,000 euros during a ceremony in Amsterdam.

He “works with quiet discretion, preferring to remain out of the limelight while working from his base in Kumasi,” the fund said.

item.title: November set to be coldest in almost 30 years after record night
item.description:
November set to be coldest in almost 30 years after record night

November 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

This November is on course to be the coldest in the Netherlands since 1998, after many weather stations recorded their coldest November 27 night on record, broadcaster NOS reported on Friday.

The temperature in Twente dropped to -8.1° overnight, and 26 other stations also set a new cold record for the date, NOS said.

The month has had an unusually high number of frost nights. The normal November average is around 7°, according to weather forecaster Weerplaza.

Temperatures will stay around or just above freezing on Friday, with sunshine all day and a moderate easterly wind. In some places the temperature may not rise above zero at all.

The cold has made natural ice skating possible in several places. The first marathon on natural ice was held in Winterswijk on Thursday evening, won by Jade Groenewoud in the women’s race and Christiaan Haasjes in the men’s.

Friday night will be cold again, with lows of -4° to -7°. Temperatures will rise slightly on Saturday and there will be more cloud. Sunday will be wet, with highs of 2° to 5°, and the rain may start as wet snow.

item.title: Missile mural appears on Dutch embassy in Moscow
item.description:
Missile mural appears on Dutch embassy in Moscow

November 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A mural appeared on the outer wall of the Dutch embassy in Moscow on Thursday, depicting flying missiles with the words “flowers of Dutch diplomacy” written in their blast trail.

The mural, for which no one has claimed responsibility, appeared days after the dispute over Dutch defence company Destinus, who publicised the use of its weapons on the Crimea bridge.

The Russian embassy in The Hague was quick to respond that staff from the company may be considered legitimate military targets if so and asked if The Hague was “joining the conflict”.

A subsequent investigation by the NRC found that Destinus employees may have been personally engaging in drone battles.

Shortly after, the Dutch embassy in Kyiv was struck during a barrage of drone strikes. Whether the building was an intended target remains unclear.

Prime minister Rob Jetten said the Netherlands would not be intimidated by Russian threats.

The Russian embassy has lodged a formal request for clarification over the involvement of Destinus staff in the conflict.

item.title: Ajax, AZ and NEC all win in European football
item.description:
Ajax, AZ and NEC all win in European football

November 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Ajax, AZ and NEC all won their European matches on Thursday evening, with NEC moving into the Europa League’s automatic qualification places.

Ajax beat Swiss side FC Thun 4-0 at the Johan Cruijff Arena in the Conference League. It is the Amsterdam club’s third win in a row after an opening defeat at Hajduk Split, and it lifts them to third place for now, with other matches still being played.

The top eight after six rounds go straight through to the last 16.

AZ came back from 2-0 down at half-time to win 4-2 at Sparta Prague in the Europa League.

NEC beat French side Stade Rennais 3-1 at De Goffert in Nijmegen. NEC are now eighth in the Europa League table with 10 points, a position that would give them a direct place in the last 16.

item.title: More young people are on social benefits in NL
item.description:
More young people are on social benefits in NL

November 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The number of young people receiving benefits is up over last year, according to new figures by the Dutch statistics agency.

The CBS found that 43,000 people aged under 27 were on welfare at the end of September, an increase of 6.3% over 2025.

In the second quarter of 2026, the number of young people receiving assistance was also up, by 5.6%, compared to a year earlier.

The number of recipients also increased in the 27 to 45-year-old bracket, but only by 1.2% compared to a year earlier.

For those aged 45 to state pension age, the number of people receiving social benefits decreased by 0.1%.

Overall, 411,000 people were receiving a social assistance benefit at the end of September, an increase of 4,000 over 2025.
